abstract: Spectroscopy of dried, ground foliage is a cost-efficient measurement to estimate leaf biochemical traits in agricultural and ecological research. Drying removes water that obscures biochemical absorption features, and milling homogenizes samples, yet how drying and milling methods affect spectra and trait predictions is understudied. We compared two drying methods (oven-drying; flash-freezing then freeze-drying) and three milling methods (coarse and fine rotary milling; ball milling) using 61 individuals of 11 broadleaf and needle- or scale-leaved woody species. Mean reflectance differences between milling treatments ranged 1.7-4.6% across the full spectrum and were largest between fine and coarse rotary milling. Freeze-dried samples had on average 7.2% higher reflectance than oven-dried samples, with larger differences in broadleaf species. Bayesian ANOVAs of spectrally predicted nitrogen and calcium demonstrated that drying had the largest effect, and that fine and ball milling also shifted predictions relative to coarse milling, but all treatment effects were smaller than interspecific variation. Although the partial least squares regression models were trained on oven-dried material, freeze-dried and more finely milled samples had lower prediction error (NRMSE) than oven-dried samples. Our finding emphasize that sample processing methods should be carefully documented for studies measuring traits from foliar spectroscopy.
